Latent Dirichlet Allocation Notebook¶

This notebook file contains Python Cells that enable the user to perform Latent Dirichlet Allocaiton (LDA) on a dataset containing texts of any length. LDA is a probabilistic model originally designed to generate text. As a means to model topics/ideas in a dataset, LDA is reverse engineered to model documents (text) as a mixture of topics (e.g., it might model a document as 60% related to sports and 40% related to finance) and topics (ideas) as a mixture of words (e.g., it might model sports as 20% football, 8% soccer, etc.).

This Notebook is broken into five different Parts: Part 1: (Importing and Installing what's needed to do everything else) Part 2: Loading and Preprocessing Data (all preprocessing steps are optional -- if you would like to skip one or more preprocessing steps, simply change the column names (inside '') of the data being processed by a cell to the column name of the previous preprpocessing step. Part 3: Converting the preprocessed text data into numbers (word embedding; Part 4: Creating the LDA model and looking at the document-topic distribution (mixture of topics in each document) and topic-word distribution (mixture of words in each topic); and Part 5: Visualization and Calculating Performance

#Expand Contractions (e.g., don't becomes do not)
import contractions
#Define function that expands contractions in a single string of text
def expand_contractions_text(text):
    if isinstance(text, str):
        # contractions.fix() handles the entire string/sentence
        expanded_text = contractions.fix(text)
        return expanded_text
    return text

#Apply the function to all of the texts in "LowerCase" column of the dataframe
data_reduced['ExpandContractions'] = data_reduced['TAReplaced'].apply(expand_contractions_text)

#Print Expaneded Data for Sanity Checking
print (data_reduced['ExpandContractions'])

import string

def remove_punctuation(text):
    """Removes punctuation from a string."""
    return ''.join([char for char in text if char not in string.punctuation])

#Apply the function to all of the texts in "ExpandContractions" column of the dataframe

#Model Topics in dataset with Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)

#Create empty dataframe for Results
lda_results = pd.DataFrame()

#This cell uses the document term matrix (doc_term)
#which was created in the previosu cell via word embedding
#doc-term represens the words in the dataset as numbers
#rows are documents
#columns are words in the vocabulary (i.e., all words found in the preprocessed dataset)

#Set primary model hyperparameters
n_topics = 3
default_alpha = 1/n_topics
default_beta = 1/n_topics

#Explanation of hyperparameters:
#n_components = number of topics
#doc_topics_prior = value of alpha for dirichlet distribution of documents and topics)
#small alpha leads to fewer documents having the same topics
#large alpha leads to many documents having the same topics

#topic_word_prior = value of beta for dirichelt distribution of topics and words)
#large beta leads to more words being assigned to multiple topics
#small beta leads to fewer words being assigned to multiple topics

#learning_decay = how much the learning rate decreases with each iteration of LDA (bigger value means faster convergence)
#batch_size = parameters that influneces tradeoff between speed and convergence (higher value is faster but may not converge)
#max_iter = number of interations of LDA/Bayes algorithm; default is 10

#Create LDA Model
#Adjust n_components, doc_topic_prior, topic_word_prior as needed to optimize model
LDA_model = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=n_topics, doc_topic_prior=default_alpha, topic_word_prior=default_beta, learning_decay=0.7, batch_size=50, max_iter=10)
LDA_model.fit(doc_term)

topic_word_distributions = LDA_model.components_

#Initiate topics
k = topic_word_distributions.shape[0]
topics = [None]*k

#Map the numebrs in LDA_model.components_ back to words
feature_names = embedded_data.get_feature_names_out()#Retrieve the top (most frequently occurring) words for each topic
n_top_words = 8  # Number of top words to display per topic

#Print the n_top_words per topic
for topic_idx, topic in enumerate(topic_word_distributions):
    # Sort words by their strength in the current topic and get their indices
    top_word_indices = topic.argsort()[:-n_top_words-1:-1]
    # Map indices back to words
    top_words = [feature_names[i] for i in top_word_indices]
    topics[topic_idx] = top_words
    print(f"Topic {topic_idx}: {' '.join(top_words)}")

top_words_topics = topics[0:n_topics]

In [105]:
#Fifth set of LDA Results:  Calculate Topic Coherence (UMass)

#Topic Coherence is an internal performance metric
#thst measures whether the top keywords assigned to a topic actually belong together logically
#Umass calculatesthe log-conditional likelihood of co-occurrence between the top words in a topic,
#It captures how often pairs of words (wi, wj) occur in the same documents (co-occurence)
#relative to how often the single word wi appears
#UMass scores are usually negative; the less negative the "better" the topic coherence

corpus_documents = data_reduced.loc[:, 'NoStopWords'].str.split()

#The following function calculates the parameters necessry to calculate UMass
def calculate_umass_coherence(topics, corpus_documents):
    """
    Calculates UMass topic coherence manually.

    Args:
        topics (list of list of str): A list where each inner list represents a topic
                                      and contains its top words.
        corpus_documents (list of list of str): A list where each inner list represents
                                                a document and contains its tokens.

    Returns:
        float: The average UMass coherence score across all topics.
    """

    # 1. Calculate D(w) and D(w_i, w_j)
    doc_freq = defaultdict(int)
    co_occurrence_freq = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(int))

    for doc in corpus_documents:
        unique_words_in_doc = list(set(doc)) # Consider only unique words per document for D(w) and D(w_i, w_j)
        for i, word_i in enumerate(unique_words_in_doc):
            doc_freq[word_i] += 1
            for j in range(i + 1, len(unique_words_in_doc)):
                word_j = unique_words_in_doc[j]
                co_occurrence_freq[word_i][word_j] += 1
                co_occurrence_freq[word_j][word_i] += 1 # Symmetric

    topic_coherence_scores = []
    for topic_words in topics:
        topic_pmi_sum = 0
        pair_count = 0

        # Calculate PMI for all unique pairs within the topic
        for i, word_i in enumerate(topic_words):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(topic_words)):
                word_j = topic_words[j]

                # Ensure words are in our corpus and have frequencies
                if word_i in doc_freq and word_j in doc_freq:
                    # Smoothing: Add 1 to co-occurrence if it's zero
                    co_occurrence = co_occurrence_freq[word_i][word_j]

                    # UMass uses log((D(w_i, w_j) + 1) / (D(w_i) * D(w_j)))
                    # Note: Gensim's UMass uses log((D(w_i, w_j) + 1) / D(w_i)) in some contexts,
                    # but the general formula includes D(w_j) in the denominator.
                    # The exact formula can vary slightly across implementations.

                    # For a common UMass variant, we use: log((D(w_i, w_j) + 1) / D(w_i))
                    # This is often the Gensim-like approach for UMass.
                    if doc_freq[word_i] > 0: # Avoid division by zero
                        pmi = math.log((co_occurrence + 1) / doc_freq[word_i])
                        topic_pmi_sum += pmi
                        pair_count += 1

        if pair_count > 0:
            topic_coherence_scores.append(topic_pmi_sum / pair_count)
        else:
            topic_coherence_scores.append(0) # Or handle as appropriate

    if topic_coherence_scores:
        return topic_coherence_scores, sum(topic_coherence_scores) / len(topic_coherence_scores)
        #return sum(topic_coherence_scores) / len(topic_coherence_scores)
    else:
        return 0.0
#End of Function

# Calculating UMass by Topic for a simple example
# To Sanity check the function above and also to understand better what UMass is doing
corpus_example = [
     ["apple", "banana", "fruit"],
     ["apple", "orange", "fruit"],
     ["car", "truck", "vehicle"],

 ]
topics_example = [

]

print (corpus_example)
print ()
print ("The top words for the two topics discovered in the sample dataset are: ",)
print (topics_example)
print ()
coherence = calculate_umass_coherence(topics_example, corpus_example)
print("UMass Topic Coherence for the two topics in the example dataset, followed by average coherence: ")
print(f"UMass Coherence {coherence}")
print ()

print ()
print ("Coherence Calculations for the data modelled by LDA in this notebook:")
print ("The top words in the topics discovered in LDA processed dataset are: ",)
print (top_words_topics)
print ()
# The following returns the Umass Coherence values for each topic and the aggregate Umass topic coherence

print("The UMass Coherence for the topics in the LDA processed dataset, followed by average coherence: ")
print(f"UMass Coherence {coherence}")

Homework 4 (Task 1): UMass Topic Coherence vs. Number of Topics¶

In [106]:
#Part 6C:  Choosing the Number of Topics -- Perplexity and Coherence Curves
#Fits LDA for a range of topic counts (this cell can take a minute or two)
#Note: scikit-learn's perplexity is only a rough guide when the input is TF-IDF (not raw counts) and is
#computed on the training data, so it can rise with more topics; weigh it together with coherence.
#For raw word counts, switch Part 3 to CountVectorizer for a more meaningful perplexity.
k_values = list(range(2, 11))
perplexities, coherences = [], []

for k in k_values:
    m = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=k, doc_topic_prior=1/k, topic_word_prior=1/k,
                                  learning_decay=0.7, batch_size=50, max_iter=10, random_state=0)
    m.fit(doc_term)
    perplexities.append(m.perplexity(doc_term))
    top = [[feature_names[i] for i in comp.argsort()[:-n_top_words-1:-1]] for comp in m.components_]
    coherences.append(calculate_umass_coherence(top, corpus_documents)[1])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
axes[0].plot(k_values, perplexities, marker='o')
axes[0].set_title('Perplexity vs Number of Topics (lower is better)')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Number of topics')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Perplexity')
axes[1].plot(k_values, coherences, marker='o', color='tab:green')
axes[1].set_title('Average UMass Coherence vs Number of Topics (higher is better)')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Number of topics')
axes[1].set_ylabel('UMass coherence')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(pd.DataFrame({'n_topics': k_values, 'perplexity': np.round(perplexities, 1), 'umass_coherence': np.round(coherences, 3)}).to_string(index=False))
print(f"Best coherence at k = {k_values[int(np.argmax(coherences))]}")

#Fifth set of LDA Results:  Calculate Topic Coherence (UMass)

#Topic Coherence is an internal performance metric
#thst measures whether the top keywords assigned to a topic actually belong together logically
#Umass calculatesthe log-conditional likelihood of co-occurrence between the top words in a topic,
#It captures how often pairs of words (wi, wj) occur in the same documents (co-occurence)
#relative to how often the single word wi appears
#UMass scores are usually negative; the less negative the "better" the topic coherence

corpus_documents = data_reduced.loc[:, 'NoStopWords'].str.split()

#The following function calculates the parameters necessry to calculate UMass
def calculate_umass_coherence(topics, corpus_documents):
    """
    Calculates UMass topic coherence manually.

    Args:
        topics (list of list of str): A list where each inner list represents a topic
                                      and contains its top words.
        corpus_documents (list of list of str): A list where each inner list represents
                                                a document and contains its tokens.

    Returns:
        float: The average UMass coherence score across all topics.
    """

    # 1. Calculate D(w) and D(w_i, w_j)
    doc_freq = defaultdict(int)
    co_occurrence_freq = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(int))

    for doc in corpus_documents:
        unique_words_in_doc = list(set(doc)) # Consider only unique words per document for D(w) and D(w_i, w_j)
        for i, word_i in enumerate(unique_words_in_doc):
            doc_freq[word_i] += 1
            for j in range(i + 1, len(unique_words_in_doc)):
                word_j = unique_words_in_doc[j]
                co_occurrence_freq[word_i][word_j] += 1
                co_occurrence_freq[word_j][word_i] += 1 # Symmetric

    topic_coherence_scores = []
    for topic_words in topics:
        topic_pmi_sum = 0
        pair_count = 0

        # Calculate PMI for all unique pairs within the topic
        for i, word_i in enumerate(topic_words):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(topic_words)):
                word_j = topic_words[j]

                # Ensure words are in our corpus and have frequencies
                if word_i in doc_freq and word_j in doc_freq:
                    # Smoothing: Add 1 to co-occurrence if it's zero
                    co_occurrence = co_occurrence_freq[word_i][word_j]

                    # UMass uses log((D(w_i, w_j) + 1) / (D(w_i) * D(w_j)))
                    # Note: Gensim's UMass uses log((D(w_i, w_j) + 1) / D(w_i)) in some contexts,
                    # but the general formula includes D(w_j) in the denominator.
                    # The exact formula can vary slightly across implementations.

                    # For a common UMass variant, we use: log((D(w_i, w_j) + 1) / D(w_i))
                    # This is often the Gensim-like approach for UMass.
                    if doc_freq[word_i] > 0: # Avoid division by zero
                        pmi = math.log((co_occurrence + 1) / doc_freq[word_i])
                        topic_pmi_sum += pmi
                        pair_count += 1

        if pair_count > 0:
            topic_coherence_scores.append(topic_pmi_sum / pair_count)
        else:
            topic_coherence_scores.append(0) # Or handle as appropriate

    if topic_coherence_scores:
        return topic_coherence_scores, sum(topic_coherence_scores) / len(topic_coherence_scores)
        #return sum(topic_coherence_scores) / len(topic_coherence_scores)
    else:
        return 0.0
#End of Function

# Calculating UMass by Topic for a simple example
# To Sanity check the function above and also to understand better what UMass is doing
corpus_example = [
     ["apple", "banana", "fruit"],
     ["apple", "orange", "fruit"],
     ["car", "truck", "vehicle"],
     ["banana", "smoothie"],
 ]
topics_example = [

]

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from gensim.models.coherencemodel import CoherenceModel
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
from gensim.corpora import Dictionary

#Set range of topics
topic_nums = range(2, 11)
coherence_scores = []

# # 1. Vectorize corpus to get a document-term matrix

# feature_names = vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()

#Create the Gensim dictionary needed for mapping
tokenized_corpus = [doc.lower().split() for doc in text_corpus]
dictionary = Dictionary(tokenized_corpus)

#feature_names = vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()
n_top_words = 4  # Number of words to evaluate per topic
topics = []

for k in topic_nums:
  #Create LSA Model
  lsa_model = TruncatedSVD(n_components=k, random_state=42)
  lsa_model.fit(doc_term)
  for topic_idx, topic in enumerate(lsa_model.components_):
      # Get the indices of the top words sorted by weight
      top_features_ind = topic.argsort()[:-n_top_words - 1:-1]
      top_words = [feature_names[i] for i in top_features_ind]
      topics.append(top_words)

  #Use Gensim's CoherenceModel to calculate the score
  coherence_model = CoherenceModel(
    topics=topics,          # Pass the manually extracted top words
    texts=tokenized_corpus,            # Pass the tokenized corpus for co-occurrence counting
    dictionary=dictionary,  # Pass the Gensim dictionary
    coherence='u_mass'         # Choose coherence metric ('c_v', 'u_mass', etc.)
  )
  coherence_score = coherence_model.get_coherence()
  print(f"LSA Topic Coherence Score (Umass): {coherence_score:.4f}")
  coherence_scores.append(coherence_model.get_coherence())

#Strong vs. weak:  margin = highest topic probability (max_prob, as in Part 6A) minus the second-highest topic probability
strong_threshold = 0.60
weak_threshold = 0.10

prob_cols = [c for c in lda_results.columns if c.startswith('Topic Probability_')]
max_prob = lda_results[prob_cols].max(axis=1).values
second_prob = np.sort(lda_results[prob_cols].values, axis=1)[:, -2]
lda_results['Second Topic'] = np.argsort(lda_results[prob_cols].values, axis=1)[:, -2]
lda_results['Margin'] = max_prob - second_prob

#Documents with no words left in the vocabulary get equal probabilities for every topic; they are
#reported separately because there is nothing for LDA to model, rather than counted as weak
lda_results['Words in Vocabulary'] = np.diff(doc_term.tocsr().indptr)
empty_doc = (lda_results['Words in Vocabulary'] == 0).values
lda_results['Assignment'] = np.select([empty_doc, lda_results['Margin'] >= strong_threshold, lda_results['Margin'] < weak_threshold],
                                      ['Empty (no vocabulary words)', 'Strong', 'Weak'], default='In between')

temp1_df = data_reduced.reset_index(drop=True)
output_df = pd.concat([temp1_df['OriginalResponse'], lda_results], axis=1)

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
n_examples = 5

def pick_varied(candidates, key, max_topic_uses):
    picked, used_keys, topic_uses = [], set(), Counter()
    for i, row in candidates.sample(frac=1, random_state=rng).iterrows():
        k = key(row)
        topics_in_row = [row['Dominant Topic'], row['Second Topic']] if max_topic_uses else []
        if k in used_keys or any(topic_uses[t] >= max_topic_uses for t in topics_in_row):
            continue
        picked.append(i)
        used_keys.add(k)
        topic_uses.update(topics_in_row)
        if len(picked) == n_examples:
            break
    return output_df.loc[picked]

long_enough = output_df['Words in Vocabulary'] >= 4
strong_examples = pick_varied(output_df[(output_df['Assignment'] == 'Strong') & long_enough],
                              key=lambda r: r['Dominant Topic'], max_topic_uses=0)
weak_examples = pick_varied(output_df[(output_df['Assignment'] == 'Weak') & long_enough],
                            key=lambda r: frozenset((r['Dominant Topic'], r['Second Topic'])), max_topic_uses=2)

for name, examples in (('Strong', strong_examples), ('Weak', weak_examples)):
    print(f'"{name}" Topic Assignment Examples')
    print('-' * 100)
    for i, row in examples.iterrows():
        probs = '  '.join(f'T{t}: {row[c]:.2f}' for t, c in enumerate(prob_cols))
        print(f"[Doc {i}] Dominant topic {row['Dominant Topic']}, margin {row['Margin']:.3f}")
        print(f"  {row['OriginalResponse'].strip()}")
        print(f"  {probs}")
        print()

    weak_examples[['OriginalResponse'] + prob_cols + ['Margin']].to_excel(writer, sheet_name='Weak', index_label='Doc')

#Word clouds for each topic of the k = 6 LDA Model (LDA_model) from Part 1b
n_wc_words = 20   #number of words shown in each word cloud
n_pool_words = 30 #number of top words considered per topic (extra words replace any that are removed later)

#Get the top n_pool_words words (and their weights) for each topic
feature_names = embedded_data.get_feature_names_out()
top_words_per_topic_wc = []
for topic_idx, topic in enumerate(LDA_model.components_):
    top_words_indices = topic.argsort()[-n_pool_words:][::-1] # Get indices of top n_pool_words words
    top_words = []
    for i in top_words_indices:
        top_words.append((feature_names[i], topic[i]))
    top_words_per_topic_wc.append(top_words)

#Count how many topics each word appears in (within each topic's top n_pool_words words)
min_shared_topics = 4
word_topic_counts = Counter()
for topic_words in top_words_per_topic_wc:
    for word, weight in topic_words:
        word_topic_counts[word] += 1

#Words found in min_shared_topics or more topics are removed from every word cloud
shared_words = set()
for word, count in word_topic_counts.items():
    if count >= min_shared_topics:
        shared_words.add(word)

print(f"Removed from every word cloud (in the top {n_pool_words} words of {min_shared_topics}+ topics): {sorted(shared_words)}")
print()

#Words removed from individual topics because they clearly belong to a different topic
#Modify (add, remove) words as needed/desired
custom_remove = {
    0: {'example', 'problem'},              #worked examples belong to Topic 4
    1: {'time'},                            #generic
    2: {'office', 'hour', 'material', 'make', 'know', 'think'},  #office hours belong to Topic 1; course material belongs to Topic 5; generic words
    3: {'work', 'know', 'make'},            #generic
    4: {'material', 'learn', 'thing'},      #course material belongs to Topic 5; generic words
    5: {'example', 'teach', 'understand'},  #worked examples belong to Topic 4; generic words
}

cleaned_words_per_topic_wc = []
for topic_idx, topic_words in enumerate(top_words_per_topic_wc):
    #Words to remove from this topic = shared words + this topic's custom words
    remove = shared_words | custom_remove.get(topic_idx, set())

    #Words that would have appeared in this topic's word cloud but were removed
    removed = []
    for word, weight in topic_words[:n_wc_words]:
        if word in remove:
            removed.append(word)

    #Keep every word (and its weight) that is not being removed
    cleaned_words = []
    for word, weight in topic_words:
        if word not in remove:
            cleaned_words.append((word, weight))
    cleaned_words_per_topic_wc.append(cleaned_words)

    #Words that now appear in this topic's word cloud
    shown_words = []
    for word, weight in cleaned_words[:n_wc_words]:
        shown_words.append(word)

    print(f"Topic {topic_idx}: removed {removed}")
    print(f"         now shows {' '.join(shown_words)}")

#Plot one word cloud per topic, in a grid of 2 rows x 3 columns
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 8))
axes = axes.flatten()
for i, topic_words in enumerate(cleaned_words_per_topic_wc):
    # Create a dictionary of words and their weights/frequencies
    word_freq_dict = {}
    for word, weight in topic_words[:n_wc_words]:
        word_freq_dict[word] = weight
    wordcloud = WordCloud(width=800, height=400, background_color='white').generate_from_frequencies(word_freq_dict)
    axes[i].imshow(wordcloud, interpolation='bilinear')
    axes[i].set_title(f'Topic {i} Word Cloud')
    axes[i].axis('off')
fig.suptitle('LDA Topic Word Clouds (k = 6), Shared and Borrowed Words Removed', fontsize=16)

#Calculate Reconstruction Error
#If optimal number of topics is desired, run this cell in a loop
#In combination with the nmf model generated in Part 4
#(difference between original word embedded matrix and W*H)
reconstruction_errors = []
for k in topic_nums:
  #Create NMF Model
  nmf_model = NMF(
      n_components=k,  # Number of latent components (rank)
      init="nndsvdar",  # Initialization method ('random', 'nndsvd', 'nndsvda', 'nndsvdar', 'custom')
      solver="cd",  # Numerical solver: 'cd' (Coordinate Descent) or 'mu' (Multiplicative Update)
      beta_loss="frobenius",  # Beta divergence ('frobenius', 'kullback-leibler', 'itakura-saito')
      tol=1e-4,  # Stopping tolerance for convergence
      max_iter=500,  # Maximum number of iterations
      random_state=42,  # Seed for random number generation
      alpha_W=0.0,  # L1/L2 regularization penalty for matrix W
      alpha_H=0.0,  # L1/L2 regularization penalty for matrix H ('same' uses alpha_W)
      l1_ratio=0.5,  # Trade-off between L1 and L2 regularization (0 = pure L2, 1 = pure L1)
      verbose=0,  # Verbosity flag (0 for silent, >0 for progress output)
      shuffle=False,  # Whether to randomize coordinate order in CD solver
  )
  nmf_model.fit(doc_term)
  reconstruction_error = nmf_model.reconstruction_err_
  print(f"Reconstruction error (scikit-learn): {reconstruction_error}")
  reconstruction_errors.append(reconstruction_error)

#Plot the results
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(topic_nums, reconstruction_errors, marker='o', linestyle='-', color='b')
plt.xlabel('Number of Topics ($k$)')
plt.ylabel('Reconstruction Error')

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

n_top_words = 10
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, kTopics, figsize=(18, 5), sharex=False)
axes = axes.flatten()

for topic_idx, topic in enumerate(lsa_model.components_):
    top_features_ind = topic.argsort()[: -n_top_words - 1 : -1]
    top_features = feature_names[top_features_ind]
    weights = topic[top_features_ind]

    ax = axes[topic_idx]
    ax.barh(top_features, weights, color='skyblue', edgecolor='navy')
    ax.set_title(f'Topic {topic_idx + 1}', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    ax.invert_yaxis()  # Put the highest-scoring word at the top
    ax.tick_params(axis='both', which='major', labelsize=11)

    if topic_idx == 0:
        ax.set_xlabel('Word Weight', fontsize=12)

plt.suptitle('Top Word Frequencies (Weights) Per LSA Topic', fontsize=18, fontweight='bold', y=1.05)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

#Each row in NMF.components_ represents a topic and the numbers in the row represent how many times a word occurs for that topic
topic_word_distributions = nmf_model.components_

#Initiate topics
k = topic_word_distributions.shape[0]
topics = [None]*k

#Map the numebrs in NMF_model.components_ back to words
feature_names = embedded_data.get_feature_names_out()#Retrieve the top (most frequently occurring) words for each topic
n_top_words = 8  # Number of top words to display per topic

#Print the n_top_words per topic
for topic_idx, topic in enumerate(topic_word_distributions):
    # Sort words by their strength in the current topic and get their indices
    top_word_indices = topic.argsort()[:-n_top_words-1:-1]
    # Map indices back to words
    top_words = [feature_names[i] for i in top_word_indices]
    topics[topic_idx] = top_words
    print(f"Topic {topic_idx}: {' '.join(top_words)}")

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import NMF
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from wordcloud import WordCloud

#Initialize the plot grid (e.g., 2 rows, 3 columns to fit 5 subplots nicely)
#Adjust to suit the number of topics given in kTopics in the nmf_model
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 10))
axes = axes.flatten()  # Flatten the 2D array to iterate easily

# 5. Extract topic weights and generate word clouds
for topic_idx, topic in enumerate(nmf_model.components_):
    # Create a dictionary mapping the feature name to its continuous NMF weight
    word_freqs = {
        feature_names[i]: topic[i]
        for i in range(len(feature_names))
        if topic[i] > 0
    }

    # Generate the word cloud using the weights as custom frequencies
    wordcloud = WordCloud(
        width=600, height=400, background_color="white", colormap="viridis"
    ).generate_from_frequencies(word_freqs)

    # Plot the word cloud in its respective subplot slot
    ax = axes[topic_idx]
    ax.imshow(wordcloud, interpolation="bilinear")
    ax.set_title(f"Topic {topic_idx + 1}", fontsize=16, fontweight="bold")
    ax.axis("off")

# Hide any unused subplots (the 6th slot in our 2x3 grid)
for idx in range(kTopics, len(axes)):
    fig.delaxes(axes[idx])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
